title: Mead Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Mead wells have a 22 ft median depth, but records range to 1,000 ft. See yield, water levels, drilling costs and buyer risks.
h1: What Mead, Colorado Well Records Show Buyers
intro_html:
Well records within five miles of Mead show a mostly shallow plains setting, but the local range is wide. The median reported depth is 22 feet, and the middle half runs from 15 to 39 feet. Some wells reach 1,000 feet.

That spread matters when you are pricing a rural property or planning a new build. Reported yields are generally strong, with a 15.0 gallon-per-minute median, but the available testing data is limited. The records include 1,038 permitted wells, while only 538 are recorded as constructed and 73 report a pump yield.

sections.heading: Mead well depth depends on the local formation
sections.html:
Mead’s permitted wells are associated mainly with Denver Basin aquifers and unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. The records identify Denver Basin aquifer wells as 62% of the total, with 694 wells tied to unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers and 122 tied to alluvial aquifers.

Most reported wells are shallow: 90% are under 100 feet. The middle half falls between 15 and 39 feet, which gives a driller a useful starting point for a bid, not a guaranteed finished depth. Six percent are 100 to 300 feet, 4% are 300 to 600 feet, and 1% exceed 600 feet. A 1,000-foot record shows why a neighboring well is more useful than a countywide guess.

sections.heading: Expected well yield around Mead
sections.html:
The reported yield median is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 65.0 gallons per minute. Among the 73 wells that report a pump yield, 58% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 30% fall from 5 to 15 gallons per minute.

Low-producing wells are present but uncommon in this record: 11% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute and 1% report under 1 gallon per minute. Treat those figures as local context, not a promise for a particular lot. Ask for the well construction report, pump test, permitted use, storage capacity and any production limitations before relying on the water for a house, livestock or irrigation.

sections.heading: Mead water levels and what the record suggests
sections.html:
Reported static water levels are shallow. The median depth to water is 9 feet, and the middle half runs from 6 to 12 feet below the surface. That can reduce pumping lift, but it also means excavation, casing, grout and surface drainage deserve careful attention.

The decade series does not show a dropping table in these records. The median measured water level was 12 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 8 feet in the 2020s, meaning the later reported measurements were closer to the surface. Measurements come from only 90 wells, so do not use the series as a guarantee for a specific parcel. A current measurement and a nearby well history are better checks.

sections.heading: Permit history shows continuing Mead activity
sections.html:
Mead has a long permit record, with permits issued from the 1950s through the 2020s and the newest permit year listed as 2026. The busiest decades in the records were the 2000s, with 246 permits, and the 2020s, with 196. That history gives buyers more neighboring records to compare than a recently developed area would.

The database lists 1,038 permitted wells, but only 538 as constructed. Use the Colorado Division of Water Resources permit and construction documents to confirm that an existing well was actually completed, what it may legally serve, and whether the permit matches the property. The most active listed driller is Authorized (Pe, Pg), followed by Terracon Consultants Inc. (Rogers, Richard C.) and Marshall Drilling (Marshall, James C.).

sections.heading: What drilling a Mead well can cost
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 22-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone models to about $1,100 to $1,500. That is not the price of a usable water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $7,100 to $13,500. A contractor’s actual bid can change with access, casing and grout requirements, pump size, power availability, water treatment and the final depth. A shallow result may still need substantial site work. Get the drilling scope and the complete well-system scope in writing so the low per-foot rate does not hide omitted work.

sections.heading: Mead risks to check before you close
sections.html:
Low yield and dry-hole risk cannot be ruled out by the local median. The records include wells under 1 gallon per minute, and the 1,000-foot maximum shows that depth can vary sharply. Fractured-bedrock conditions are especially unpredictable because a nearby hole may not intersect the same water-bearing fractures.

Water quality also needs a property-specific test. Mapped environmental information within about 10 miles includes 1,163 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 8 historic mine features and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped sites do not prove contamination at a parcel, but they are a reason to test for the contaminants relevant to the location. Check septic setbacks, soil, drainage, building-envelope space and the legal water use before buying or designing.

sections.heading: A practical Mead lot-buying plan
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then compare nearby DWR records rather than relying on the Mead median. Look for reported depth, static water level, yield, aquifer name, construction status and permitted use. Berthoud, Firestone, Johnstown, Longmont, Platteville and Frederick provide broader regional context, but a well beside the lot is the stronger comparison.

For an existing home, request the permit, construction report, pump information, water-quality results and maintenance history. For vacant land, confirm that a new well can be permitted for the intended household use and that the septic system, driveway and building site can fit together. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required for some uses. Have a Colorado well contractor and the appropriate county or water officials review the plan before closing.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Mead, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Mead is 22 feet, with the middle half between 15 and 39 feet. Ninety percent are under 100 feet, but the record ranges to 1,000 feet. That wide range means nearby well logs and the specific aquifer matter more than the median when estimating a new well.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Mead?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 22-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $1,100 to $1,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $7,100 to $13,500. Access, final depth, equipment and site conditions can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Mead wells produce?
faq.a: Reported yields have a 15.0 gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 10.0 to 65.0 gallons per minute. Among wells reporting yield, 58% are above 15 gallons per minute, while 1% are under 1 gallon per minute. Only 73 wells report a pump yield, so these figures are not a guarantee for a lot.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Mead, Colorado?
faq.a: The well records do not establish that water is safe to drink. Test the individual well before relying on it, especially because mapped sites within about 10 miles include 1,163 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 8 historic mine features and 6 EPA cleanup sites. Those locations are screening information, not proof of contamination on a specific property.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Mead?
faq.a: The reported decade medians do not show a dropping water table. Median static water level was 12 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 8 feet in the 2020s, so later measurements were shallower. Only 90 wells report static water levels, however. A current measurement and nearby well history are more useful for a purchase decision.
